The viscosity of 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolyte is gradually increased with the PC content rising. With an increase in the PC content, the conductivity increases markedly in the range lower than 40%, reaches a maximum at 60% (i.e., PC/EMC=3/2), and inversely declines in the range higher than 60% (Fig. 1c).

crystallizes at -20 °C and completely freezes at -30 °C. Whereas PC/DMC, EC/EMC and EC/DEC electrolytes, obvious crystallization starts at -30 °C and gets severe at -40 °C. In contrast, the ionic conductivity of PC/EMC electrolyte decreases much slowly than other electrolytes and no crystallization occurs even at -40 °C (Fig.2c).

It is shown that the cell retains 82.95% (-20 °C), 74.40% (-30 °C) and 52.16% (-40 °C) capacity retentions, being moderately better than the cells with 0.8 M and 1.2 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolytes (Fig. S5).

compared to NaFSI-E, NaDFOB-E and $NaPF_{6}-E$ exhibit lower viscosity from 0 °C to high temperature of 60 °C. When the temperature drops to -10 °C, the viscosity of $NaPF_{6}-E$ rapidly increases and the saturation of NaDFOB occurs, while NaFSI-E shows lower viscosity.

Specifically, propylene carbonate (PC), with its low melting point of $-49\ ^{\circ}C$ , moderate dielectric constant of 64, and donor number of 15.1 kcal mol $^{-1}$ , not only ensures high ionic conductivity but also guarantees stable operation of SIBs under subzero conditions.

At 25 °C, 0.5-P-D exhibits a lower ionic conductivity (2.7 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) compared to 1.0-P-D (7.3 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) and 1.0-P-E/M (15.3 mS cm $^{-1}$ ) due to its low salt concentration. Over the temperature range from 25 to -50 °C, all three electrolytes display a negative correlation between ionic conductivity and temperature.

EC has a melting point of 36 °C or approximately 309 K and as such is solid at 300 K, whereas the other solvents have melting points of -4.9 °C (PC), -68 °C (DME), -44 °C (ACN), -43 °C (DEC), and 4 °C (DMC) and are liquid at 300 K.

Similarly, severe ionic conductivity drops were observed for the other liquid 1 M $LiBF_{4}-PC$ and 1 M $LiBF_{4}-DME$ systems at reduced temperatures, mainly caused by the salt precipitation or the freezing of the electrolytes. It has previously been shown from differential scanning calorimetry measurements that increasing the $NaPF_{6}$ concentration in ethylene carbonate: dimethyl carbonate (EC:DMC 1:1 wt%) from 0.3 M to 1.4 M lowers the crystallisation temperature ( $T_{c}$ ), the temperature that in practice sets the absolute lowest working and storage limit.

For example, when using $NaPF_{6}$ electrolyte in EC:DMC (3:7 wt%) between 0.4 M and 1 M, the 0.6 M solution gave the highest conductivity (6.8 mS cm $^{-1}$ ). On the other hand, a separate study found a maximum ionic conductivity of 11.2 mS cm $^{-1}$ at 1.2 M concentration in EC:DMC (1:1 wt%).

The charge transfer resistance ( $R_{ct}$ ) of PC-based cells boosts sharply with decreasing temperature, and even reaches an awful value over 117000 $\Omega$ at $-30^{\circ}C$ , indicating a huge obstacle for the transportation of sodium ions. 3. Results and discussion
Basic physical and thermochemical properties of the electrolytes were first investigated by using $NaPF_{6}$ as the solute and mixed carbonate as the solvent. Typically, cyclic PC and EC are of high dielectric constant and high viscosity, while linear EMC, DMC and DEC feature are of much lower viscosity and relatively lower dielectric constant (Table S1) [37]. The $NaPF_{6}$ was used as the solute because it has similar electrochemical properties as $LiPF_{6}$ and much better thermal stability. $NaPF_{6}$ is stable up to $\sim400\ ^{\circ}C$ , as indicated by the TG and DSC curves in Fig.1a. The little peak at about $300\ ^{\circ}C$ is the melting endothermic peak of $NaPF_{6}$ as the literature reported. [38]

a)  
![](images/18a4e118f14bcd9b1efd69c37d5f454120655ffb1bfe57936724f96b0f0f7e7d.jpg)

b)  
![](images/eaf30d1b5e0a19992bd2db3c184e7042f2c8b157e647308db85c87a705e4ca3f.jpg)

![](images/fc87db4aba4d6959bd96a3cd76cfd285917412ac56ae8e1fab63027f06d26815.jpg)  
Fig. 1. (a) TG and DSC curves of pure $NaPF_{6}$ , (b) ionic conductivity of electrolytes with various salt concentrations in PC/EMC (1/1 v/v) at 20 °C, and (c) viscosity and conductivity of 0.8M $NaPF_{6}$ electrolytes with different PC/EMC ratios at 25 °C.

We previously showed that PC/EMC (1/1, v/v) based electrolytes make SIBs have excellent cycling performance [36]. Therefore, in the present work, the PC/EMC solvent system was preferably selected to investigate the effect of solvent ratio and salt concentration. In the binary PC/EMC (1:1, v/v) system, the highest conductivity of 7.45 mS cm $^{-1}$ at 20 °C is observed at 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ (Fig. 1b). It is also found that the conductivity of electrolyte changes with the solvent ratio changing. The viscosity of 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolyte is gradually increased with the PC content rising. With an increase in the PC content, the conductivity increases markedly in the range lower than 40%, reaches a maximum at 60% (i.e., PC/EMC=3/2), and inversely declines in the range higher than 60% (Fig. 1c). On the other hand, the electrolytes with PC content lower than 40% are much easier to wet the nonpolar polypropylene-polyethylene separator. Complete wetting of the separator typically takes no more than 10 seconds, as indicated by the wetting angles and wettability in Fig. S1 and Fig. S2. Based on the above results, five 0.8 M N

From Fig. S4b, the initial Ohm internal resistance of the cells is relatively low especial with the PC/DMC and EC/DMC electrolyte because of their high ion conductivity of electrolyte. These all can be speculated that the polarization is related to the large impedance of the electrode interface. Fig. 3b shows the rate performance of pouch cells from 0.5 C to 5 C then back to 0.2 C by charging and discharging at the same C rates. At 5 C, the PC/DMC and EC/DMC electrolyte cells show higher capacity compared with the others. The good power capability of these two cells can be attributed to high ionic conductivity of the electrolytes, which results in lower charging and discharge over-potentials [34]. Though EC/DMC electrolyte has higher ionic conductivity than the PC/DMC electrolyte, its relative cell exhibits slightly worse capacity at 5 C due to the rapid cycling decay.

When the temperature drops to -10 °C, the viscosity of $NaPF_{6}-E$ rapidly increases and the saturation of NaDFOB occurs, while NaFSI-E shows lower viscosity. The change of conductivity with temperature as shown in Fig. 1g is similar to that of viscosity, and NaFSI-E shows higher conductivity with decreasing temperature. It is worth noting that although the viscosity of NaDFOB is lower than that at high and room temperatures, it is still sufficient for the normal operation of the cell. These parameter differences will provide reference for the design of SIBs with different temperature requirements.

## 配方筛选结果
已整理候选资料，当前暂缓推荐。未满足的条件列在下方。

## 候选评估
### candidate-a
评估建议：Both candidates were assessed: their 0 °C conductivity predictions (3.449 vs 3.261 mS/cm, 1σ factors 1.318 and 1.179) overlap within the tool's uncertainty, and the literature covers only volume-based binary NaPF6 carbonate systems, so neither candidate can be shown to be superior. Advice is to hold recommendation rather than prioritize either; the predictions and the general PC-rich/carbonate low-temperature considerations should instead guide a targeted experimental comparison of the two exact formulations.
任务要求与已有依据（模型语义判断，程序核验出处）：
- Candidates are NaPF6 dissolved in an EC/EMC/PC mixed-carbonate solvent with no additives.：The source describes NaPF6 as solute in mixed carbonate solvents (cyclic PC/EC with linear EMC/DMC/DEC), matching the supplied salt/solvent family; additives are absent here and none are implied. [0005_Che 等 - 2021 - Engineering optimization approach of nonaqueous electrolyte for sodium ion battery with long cycle l::sec8::child0]

Basic physical and thermochemical properties of the electrolytes were first investigated by using $NaPF_{6}$ as the solute and mixed carbonate as the solvent. Typically, cyclic PC and EC are of high dielectric constant and high viscosity, while linear EMC, DMC and DEC feature are of much lower viscosity and relatively lower dielectric constant (Table S1) [37]. The $NaPF_{6}$ was used as the solute because it has similar electrochemical properties as $LiPF_{6}$ and much better thermal stability. $NaPF_{6}$ is stable up to $\sim400\ ^{\circ}C$ , as indicated by the TG and DSC curves in Fig.1a. The little peak at about $300\ ^{\circ}C$ is the melting endothermic peak of $NaPF_{6}$ as the literature reported. [38]

We previously showed that PC/EMC (1/1, v/v) based electrolytes make SIBs have excellent cycling performance [36]. Therefore, in the present work, the PC/EMC solvent system was preferably selected to investigate the effect of solvent ratio and salt concentration. In the binary PC/EMC (1:1, v/v) system, the highest conductivity of 7.45 mS cm $^{-1}$ at 20 °C is observed at 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ (Fig. 1b). It is shown that the ionic conductivity of these electrolytes is increased in the order of EC/DMC > PC/DMC > EC/EMC > PC/EMC > EC/DEC, whereas the viscosity is changed nearly in an opposite order of EC/DEC > EC/EMC > PC/EMC > PC/DMC ≈ EC/DMC (Fig. 2a).

source_refs.raw_quote: Ethylene carbonate (EC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), $NaPF_{6}$ , NaFSI and NaDFOB were provided by the Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd. NaFSI, $NaPF_{6}$ and NaDFOB ( $\geq98\%$ ) were also provided by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd (Table S1). Three electrolytes with 0.8 M concentration were all prepared by dissolving sodium salt in a mixture of EC: EMC = 3:7, and the electrolytes were represented as X-E, where X was the lithium salt used. All electrolytes were prepared in a dry argon filled glove box with both moisture and oxygen concentrations below 0.1 ppm. $NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_{2}$ (NFM) active material was purchased from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co, Ltd, hard carbon (HC) active material was purchased from Kuraray Co Ltd. Pouch cells were assembled using a NFM cathode (120 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1C), a HC (290 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.05C) anode, and a celgard 2700 separator. For the preparation of NFM cathode, NFM, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), carbon nanotube (CNT), conductive carbon black (Super P), and Maleic acid were dispersed in N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) with a mass ratio of 94.5:1.8:1:2.5:0.2, and the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate. For the HC anode, HC, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and conductive carbon black (Super P) with a mass ratio of 95:1.5:2:1.5 were mixed and dispersed in water, and then the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate.

source_refs.raw_quote:
A B S T R A C T
Sodium salts in the electrolytes are key materials for developing high-performance sodium ion batteries (SIBs) due to their direct influences on the electrode reactions and electrolyte conductivity, and sodium fluorophosphate $(\mathrm{NaPF}_6)$ is known to be widely applied. Using $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as a comparison, this work systematically evaluates the application potential of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ , sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) and sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) from the sodium salt nature, electrolyte properties, and battery performance. It is demonstrated that NaFSI can exhibit excellent comprehensive performance and has the potential to substitute for $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ under certain conditions; NaDFOB is more suitable as an additive to improve the high-temperature performance of SIBs. In particular, $\mathrm{NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_2}$ /hard carbon (NFM/HC) SIBs with NaDFOB achieve enhanced performance than that with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ at high temperature (from $88.2\%$ to $92.4\%$ ), while low temperature performance of NaFSI-containing cells is much better than others (from $0\%$ to $85.9\%$ ).

citations.quote:
A B S T R A C T
Sodium salts in the electrolytes are key materials for developing high-performance sodium ion batteries (SIBs) due to their direct influences on the electrode reactions and electrolyte conductivity, and sodium fluorophosphate $(\mathrm{NaPF}_6)$ is known to be widely applied. Using $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as a comparison, this work systematically evaluates the application potential of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ , sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) and sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) from the sodium salt nature, electrolyte properties, and battery performance. It is demonstrated that NaFSI can exhibit excellent comprehensive performance and has the potential to substitute for $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ under certain conditions; NaDFOB is more suitable as an additive to improve the high-temperature performance of SIBs. In particular, $\mathrm{NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_2}$ /hard carbon (NFM/HC) SIBs with NaDFOB achieve enhanced performance than that with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ at high temperature (from $88.2\%$ to $92.4\%$ ), while low temperature performance of NaFSI-containing cells is much better than others (from $0\%$ to $85.9\%$ ).

In the binary PC/EMC (1:1, v/v) system, the highest conductivity of 7.45 mS cm $^{-1}$ at 20 °C is observed at 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ (Fig. 1b). It is also found that the conductivity of electrolyte changes with the solvent ratio changing. The viscosity of 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolyte is gradually increased with the PC content rising. With an increase in the PC content, the conductivity increases markedly in the range lower than 40%, reaches a maximum at 60% (i.e., PC/EMC=3/2), and inversely declines in the range higher than 60% (Fig. 1c). On the other hand, the electrolytes with PC content lower than 40% are much easier to wet the nonpolar polypropylene-polyethylene separator. Complete wetting of the separator typically takes no more than 10 seconds, as indicated by the wetting angles and wettability in Fig. S1 and Fig. S2. Based on the above results, five 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolytes were prepared by using 2 wt% FEC additive and PC/EMC, PC/DMC, EC/EMC, EC/DMC and EC/DEC mixed solvents (all having a 2:3 cyclic/linear carbonate ratio), respectively. It is shown that the ionic conductivity of these electrolytes is increased in the order of EC/DMC > PC/DMC > EC/EMC > PC/EMC > EC/DEC, whereas the viscosity is changed nearly in an opposite order of EC/DEC > EC/EMC > PC/EMC > PC/DMC ≈ EC/DMC (Fig. 2a).

evidence_ledger.quote:
A B S T R A C T
Sodium salts in the electrolytes are key materials for developing high-performance sodium ion batteries (SIBs) due to their direct influences on the electrode reactions and electrolyte conductivity, and sodium fluorophosphate $(\mathrm{NaPF}_6)$ is known to be widely applied. Using $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as a comparison, this work systematically evaluates the application potential of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ , sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) and sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) from the sodium salt nature, electrolyte properties, and battery performance. It is demonstrated that NaFSI can exhibit excellent comprehensive performance and has the potential to substitute for $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ under certain conditions; NaDFOB is more suitable as an additive to improve the high-temperature performance of SIBs. In particular, $\mathrm{NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_2}$ /hard carbon (NFM/HC) SIBs with NaDFOB achieve enhanced performance than that with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ at high temperature (from $88.2\%$ to $92.4\%$ ), while low temperature performance of NaFSI-containing cells is much better than others (from $0\%$ to $85.9\%$ ).

citations.quote:
Basic physical and thermochemical properties of the electrolytes were first investigated by using $NaPF_{6}$ as the solute and mixed carbonate as the solvent. Typically, cyclic PC and EC are of high dielectric constant and high viscosity, while linear EMC, DMC and DEC feature are of much lower viscosity and relatively lower dielectric constant (Table S1) [37]. The $NaPF_{6}$ was used as the solute because it has similar electrochemical properties as $LiPF_{6}$ and much better thermal stability. $NaPF_{6}$ is stable up to $\sim400\ ^{\circ}C$ , as indicated by the TG and DSC curves in Fig.1a. The little peak at about $300\ ^{\circ}C$ is the melting endothermic peak of $NaPF_{6}$ as the literature reported. [38]

We previously showed that PC/EMC (1/1, v/v) based electrolytes make SIBs have excellent cycling performance [36]. Therefore, in the present work, the PC/EMC solvent system was preferably selected to investigate the effect of solvent ratio and salt concentration.

citations.quote: Therefore, in the present work, the PC/EMC solvent system was preferably selected to investigate the effect of solvent ratio and salt concentration. In the binary PC/EMC (1:1, v/v) system, the highest conductivity of 7.45 mS cm $^{-1}$ at 20 °C is observed at 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ (Fig. 1b). It is also found that the conductivity of electrolyte changes with the solvent ratio changing. The viscosity of 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolyte is gradually increased with the PC content rising. With an increase in the PC content, the conductivity increases markedly in the range lower than 40%, reaches a maximum at 60% (i.e., PC/EMC=3/2), and inversely declines in the range higher than 60% (Fig. 1c). On the other hand, the electrolytes with PC content lower than 40% are much easier to wet the nonpolar polypropylene-polyethylene separator. Complete wetting of the separator typically takes no more than 10 seconds, as indicated by the wetting angles and wettability in Fig. S1 and Fig. S2. Based on the above results, five 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolytes were prepared by using 2 wt% FEC additive and PC/EMC, PC/DMC, EC/EMC, EC/DMC and EC/DEC mixed solvents (all having a 2:3 cyclic/linear carbonate ratio), respectively. It is shown that the ionic conductivity of these electrolytes is increased in the order of EC/DMC > PC/DMC > EC/EMC > PC/EMC > EC/DEC, whereas the viscosity is changed nearly in an opposite order of EC/DEC > EC/EMC > PC/EMC > PC/DMC ≈ EC/DMC (Fig. 2a).

citations.quote: Ethylene carbonate (EC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), $NaPF_{6}$ , NaFSI and NaDFOB were provided by the Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd. NaFSI, $NaPF_{6}$ and NaDFOB ( $\geq98\%$ ) were also provided by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd (Table S1). citations.quote:
A B S T R A C T
Sodium salts in the electrolytes are key materials for developing high-performance sodium ion batteries (SIBs) due to their direct influences on the electrode reactions and electrolyte conductivity, and sodium fluorophosphate $(\mathrm{NaPF}_6)$ is known to be widely applied. Using $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as a comparison, this work systematically evaluates the application potential of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ , sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) and sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) from the sodium salt nature, electrolyte properties, and battery performance. It is demonstrated that NaFSI can exhibit excellent comprehensive performance and has the potential to substitute for $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ under certain conditions; NaDFOB is more suitable as an additive to improve the high-temperature performance of SIBs. In particular, $\mathrm{NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_2}$ /hard carbon (NFM/HC) SIBs with NaDFOB achieve enhanced performance than that with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ at high temperature (from $88.2\%$ to $92.4\%$ ), while low temperature performance of NaFSI-containing cells is much better than others (from $0\%$ to $85.9\%$ ).

citations.quote: Therefore, in the present work, the PC/EMC solvent system was preferably selected to investigate the effect of solvent ratio and salt concentration. In the binary PC/EMC (1:1, v/v) system, the highest conductivity of 7.45 mS cm $^{-1}$ at 20 °C is observed at 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ (Fig. 1b). It is also found that the conductivity of electrolyte changes with the solvent ratio changing. The viscosity of 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolyte is gradually increased with the PC content rising. With an increase in the PC content, the conductivity increases markedly in the range lower than 40%, reaches a maximum at 60% (i.e., PC/EMC=3/2), and inversely declines in the range higher than 60% (Fig. 1c). On the other hand, the electrolytes with PC content lower than 40% are much easier to wet the nonpolar polypropylene-polyethylene separator. Complete wetting of the separator typically takes no more than 10 seconds, as indicated by the wetting angles and wettability in Fig. S1 and Fig. S2. Based on the above results, five 0.8 M NaPF $_{6}$ electrolytes were prepared by using 2 wt% FEC additive and PC/EMC, PC/DMC, EC/EMC, EC/DMC and EC/DEC mixed solvents (all having a 2:3 cyclic/linear carbonate ratio), respectively. It is shown that the ionic conductivity of these electrolytes is increased in the order of EC/DMC > PC/DMC > EC/EMC > PC/EMC > EC/DEC, whereas the viscosity is changed nearly in an opposite order of EC/DEC > EC/EMC > PC/EMC > PC/DMC ≈ EC/DMC (Fig. 2a).

citations.quote: Ethylene carbonate (EC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), $NaPF_{6}$ , NaFSI and NaDFOB were provided by the Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd. NaFSI, $NaPF_{6}$ and NaDFOB ( $\geq98\%$ ) were also provided by Guangzhou Tinci Materials Technology Co, Ltd (Table S1). Three electrolytes with 0.8 M concentration were all prepared by dissolving sodium salt in a mixture of EC: EMC = 3:7, and the electrolytes were represented as X-E, where X was the lithium salt used. All electrolytes were prepared in a dry argon filled glove box with both moisture and oxygen concentrations below 0.1 ppm. $NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_{2}$ (NFM) active material was purchased from Jiangsu Xiangying New Energy Technology Co, Ltd, hard carbon (HC) active material was purchased from Kuraray Co Ltd. Pouch cells were assembled using a NFM cathode (120 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.1C), a HC (290 mAh g $^{-1}$ at 0.05C) anode, and a celgard 2700 separator. For the preparation of NFM cathode, NFM, polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), carbon nanotube (CNT), conductive carbon black (Super P), and Maleic acid were dispersed in N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) with a mass ratio of 94.5:1.8:1:2.5:0.2, and the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate. For the HC anode, HC, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and conductive carbon black (Super P) with a mass ratio of 95:1.5:2:1.5 were mixed and dispersed in water, and then the slurry was coated on an aluminum substrate.

citations.quote:
A B S T R A C T
Sodium salts in the electrolytes are key materials for developing high-performance sodium ion batteries (SIBs) due to their direct influences on the electrode reactions and electrolyte conductivity, and sodium fluorophosphate $(\mathrm{NaPF}_6)$ is known to be widely applied. Using $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ as a comparison, this work systematically evaluates the application potential of $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ , sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) and sodium difluoro(oxalato)borate (NaDFOB) from the sodium salt nature, electrolyte properties, and battery performance. It is demonstrated that NaFSI can exhibit excellent comprehensive performance and has the potential to substitute for $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ under certain conditions; NaDFOB is more suitable as an additive to improve the high-temperature performance of SIBs. In particular, $\mathrm{NaNi_{1/3}Fe_{1/3}Mn_{1/3}O_2}$ /hard carbon (NFM/HC) SIBs with NaDFOB achieve enhanced performance than that with $\mathrm{NaPF_6}$ at high temperature (from $88.2\%$ to $92.4\%$ ), while low temperature performance of NaFSI-containing cells is much better than others (from $0\%$ to $85.9\%$ ).

Advice is to hold recommendation rather than prioritize either; the predictions and the general PC-rich/carbonate low-temperature considerations should instead guide a targeted experimental comparison of the two exact formulations.

[0005_Che 等 - 2021 - Engineering optimization approach of nonaqueous electrolyte for sodium ion battery with long cycle l::sec8::child0]

- Literature describing low-temperature ionic transport in NaPF6 carbonate electrolytes is used to interpret the predictions.：The source states conductivity decreases as temperature drops (Arrhenius/VTF), and that PC/EMC-based NaPF6 electrolyte shows only a slow conductivity drop with no crystallization even at -40 °C, whereas EC-based electrolytes almost do not operate below -20 °C; other work reports NaPF6 electrolyte viscosity rising sharply below -10 °C.
